h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: With fan-in-scaled init and Adam's roughly fixed per-parameter step, wide nets change their function more per step and so hit the LR instability cliff at smaller LR.
At large LR, bigger batches reduce gradient noise and the number of risky large updates, stabilizing training.
At tiny LR the fixed 243-epoch budget makes update count the bottleneck, so fewer steps from larger batches causes underfitting.
The L2 term is scaled by 1/batch_size in sklearn-style MLPs, so larger batches relieve over-shrinkage precisely when alpha is large.
Composing more layers amplifies large Adam updates into instability, so adding depth hurts most at high LR.
Large batches give few, low-noise updates per epoch, so a larger LR is both tolerated and needed to converge in budget.
Three-layer stacks reach the LR instability cliff earlier than one-layer nets, so raising LR is more harmful for them.
With per-batch penalty scaling of alpha/batch_size, small batches amplify the effective L2 strength, so raising alpha over-regularizes sooner.
Wider nets make more function-space progress per small Adam step, partially compensating for an undersized learning rate.
Deeper nets need more updates to optimize, so adding layers hurts most when large batches leave few steps in the 243-epoch budget.
